title: Thousands of Messages, One Cable

sources.title: Douglas Comer, Purdue: Networking and Internetworking Lecture Notes

sections.title: Three senders, one cable
sections.narration: Three cameras need one cable. Watch their signals combine, travel together, then separate again. Sharing works only when the receiver can identify which part belongs to each source.
sections.takeaway: Multiplexing lets independent channels share a physical resource.

sections.title: A medium is not a channel
sections.narration: The cable is one physical medium. The colored signals are different logical channels, not extra wires. Their separation rule makes several independent conversations possible on the same path.
sections.takeaway: One physical medium can carry multiple logical channels.

sections.title: Combine, carry, separate
sections.narration: A multiplexer combines the sources. The demultiplexer recovers them using the same separation rule. Compare each arriving waveform with its original: sharing should preserve the information we wanted to send.
sections.takeaway: Sharing works only if the receiving end can separate the streams.

sections.title: Read a frequency picture
sections.narration: A waveform changes over time. Frequency counts repeating cycles per second; bandwidth spans a frequency range. Now transform the moving signals into allocations along a frequency axis.
sections.takeaway: A frequency plot shows where signal energy is allocated.

sections.title: Give every stream a band
sections.narration: Frequency division gives each channel a different band. All three signals remain active simultaneously. They share the cable without taking alternating turns, because their frequency allocations can be separated.
sections.takeaway: FDM separates simultaneously active channels in frequency.

sections.title: Leave room between neighbors
sections.narration: Real filters have imperfect edges. These five-kilohertz gaps separate neighboring bands, reducing interference. Guard space is useful, but it also consumes spectrum that cannot carry our assigned channel data.
sections.takeaway: Guard bands trade usable spectrum for easier channel separation.

sections.title: Filter at the receiver
sections.narration: Follow the green channel through a bandpass filter. Frequencies in its allocation remain prominent while neighboring bands are suppressed. The receiver separates channels by frequency, rather than waiting for a time slot.
sections.takeaway: A receiver can extract one frequency allocation with suitable filtering.

sections.title: Work an FDM allocation
sections.narration: Three channels each need twenty kilohertz. Add two internal five-kilohertz guard gaps: twenty plus five plus twenty plus five plus twenty equals seventy kilohertz. Outer margins are excluded.
sections.takeaway: Three 20 kHz channels plus two 5 kHz gaps need 70 kHz.

sections.title: What happens when one is idle?
sections.narration: The green source becomes idle, but its fixed frequency allocation remains reserved. Other sources do not automatically inherit that band. A quiet channel can leave usable capacity stranded.
sections.takeaway: A fixed allocation can waste capacity when its owner has nothing to send.

sections.title: Now divide the time axis
sections.narration: Keep one shared transmission path, but change the separation rule. These colored blocks take turns through it. The receiver uses timing and agreed boundaries to recover each source in order.
sections.takeaway: TDM distinguishes channels by when they transmit.

sections.title: Assign repeating time slots
sections.narration: A sends, then B, then C. The repeating slot schedule assigns each source a transmission opportunity. Watch the combined sequence split back into three ordered streams at the receiver.
sections.takeaway: Synchronous TDM gives channels scheduled opportunities to transmit.

sections.title: Understand a TDM frame
sections.narration: One complete A-B-C cycle forms a TDM frame in this example. This use of frame describes the repeated slot structure; it does not automatically mean an Ethernet frame.
bullets: A frame contains one slot cycle
Frame here means a TDM cycle
sections.takeaway: A TDM frame groups the slots in one repeated schedule.

sections.title: Keep the schedule aligned
sections.narration: Sender and receiver must agree on slot boundaries. The moving cursor follows the same schedule at both ends. Without alignment, a receiver could assign arriving data to the wrong source.
bullets: Sender and receiver agree on slots
sections.takeaway: Slot timing must be understood at both ends.

sections.title: Work a TDM rate example
sections.narration: Each camera supplies two megabits per second. Three continuous inputs therefore require six megabits per second of useful shared capacity. Framing and synchronization overhead may require a higher physical line rate.
sections.takeaway: Three continuous 2 Mb/s streams require 6 Mb/s of useful link capacity.

sections.title: The empty-slot problem
sections.narration: B has nothing to send. Its empty outline still occupies the reserved turn, while A and C may have data waiting. A fixed schedule can waste time even when another source is busy.
sections.takeaway: Fixed TDM can leave a slot idle even when another input has data.

sections.title: Allocate turns on demand
sections.narration: Now allocate turns according to demand. Only active A and C appear in this sequence. Statistical TDM can reclaim idle capacity, but the receiver needs labels or state identifying each source.
bullets: Labels or state identify the source
sections.takeaway: Statistical sharing adapts to demand but needs coordination.

sections.title: Move from copper to fiber
sections.narration: Inside fiber, optical signals carry information. Different wavelengths can share the same physical strand. Follow the colored waves through the combined region and back to their separate outputs.
sections.takeaway: Optical fiber supports channels carried on distinct wavelengths.

sections.title: Combine different wavelengths
sections.narration: Wavelength division assigns independent optical carriers to different wavelength channels. The colors identify those channels schematically. They travel together through the fiber rather than alternating in a time schedule.
sections.takeaway: WDM combines distinct wavelength channels on a fiber.

sections.title: Separate the light again
sections.narration: The receiving optical components separate wavelengths and direct them toward the appropriate outputs. Each colored waveform returns to its own channel. Combining light is useful only when separation remains possible.
sections.takeaway: An optical demultiplexer separates wavelength channels at the destination.

sections.title: Work a WDM capacity example
sections.narration: Four wavelength channels each carry ten gigabits per second. Their aggregate raw rate is forty gigabits per second, assuming the equipment supports simultaneous operation. Application throughput also depends on overhead.
sections.takeaway: Four independent 10 Gb/s channels total 40 Gb/s before overhead.

sections.title: Sharing has physical limits
sections.narration: Watch the received waves weaken and become less clean. Attenuation, dispersion, and noise constrain real links. Multiplexing organizes available resources; it does not create unlimited capacity or remove physical impairments.
sections.takeaway: Multiplexing organizes existing resources; it does not remove physical constraints.

sections.title: Compare the three schemes
sections.narration: Compare the moving pictures. FDM separates frequency bands, TDM separates transmission times, and WDM separates optical wavelengths. Each combines independent inputs while giving the receiver a rule for recovering them.
sections.takeaway: Ask which dimension separates the channels.

sections.title: Choose with the traffic in mind
sections.narration: Continuous streams suit predictable allocations. Bursty traffic can benefit from serving active sources on demand. The useful choice depends on the medium, equipment, traffic pattern, and coordination overhead.
sections.takeaway: The useful choice depends on the medium, traffic, and coordination costs.

sections.title: Retell the separation rule
sections.narration: Retell the three separation rules as the signals move. Different frequencies, different turns, or different optical wavelengths let one physical resource carry several recoverable channels. That is the central idea of multiplexing.
sections.takeaway: One cable can support several streams when their channels remain distinguishable.
